title: 7 Christmas Mantel Mistakes That Make Your Home Look CHEAP

scenes.text: Sweetheart, the mantel is the first thing anybody sees when they walk into your living room at Christmas. It's the stage. And most people treat it like a shelf. They line up a row of little things, stick a garland on top, hang the stockings, and wonder why it looks like a yard sale instead of a magazine. I've decorated mantels for sixty years, and it takes about ten dollars to fix.
scenes.caption: LIKE A YARD SALE

scenes.text: So tonight I'm giving you seven Christmas mantel mistakes that make it look cheap, and the old-fashioned fixes that make it look like it cost a fortune. And stay with me, because the last one is a trick my mother used with candlelight that makes any mantel look beautiful at night, even if you do nothing else.
scenes.caption: SEVEN MISTAKES

scenes.text: Our house on Elm Street had a little painted wood mantel over a coal stove that didn't even work as a fireplace. But every December, my mother turned it into the most beautiful thing on the street. She used pine branches from the woods, pinecones Danny and I gathered, red apples from the cellar, and her mother's brass candlesticks. That's it. And people stopped on the sidewalk to look through our window.
scenes.query: 1950s mantel pine branches apples brass candlesticks
scenes.caption: PINE, APPLES AND BRASS

scenes.text: One year, nineteen fifty-four, the newspaper sent a photographer around town for a Christmas page. He walked past the big houses on Park Avenue with their store-bought decorations, and he knocked on our door instead. My mother's mantel was in the Mansfield News Journal on December twentieth, and she kept that clipping in her Bible for the rest of her life. In a minute I'll tell you her secret.
scenes.caption: IN THE NEWSPAPER

scenes.text: Her secret was that she didn't buy anything new, honey. She looked at what she had, and she arranged it with care. That's what most people skip. They buy more and more, and they never take the time to arrange it. Every mistake I'm going to show you tonight can be fixed with things already in your house and the woods behind it.
scenes.caption: NOTHING NEW

scenes.text: Mistake number one. Lining everything up in a straight row, all the same height, like soldiers. Your eye has nowhere to go. The fix is to build a triangle, or a gentle wave. Put your tallest thing on one end, or in the middle, and let everything step down from there. Tall candlesticks, a medium lantern, a small bowl of pinecones. Your eye travels across, and it looks designed.
scenes.caption: NOT A STRAIGHT LINE

scenes.text: And use odd numbers, honey. Three candlesticks, not two or four. Five pinecones, not six. I don't know why it works, but it does. My mother said even numbers look like a store display, and odd numbers look like a home. She was right about most things.
scenes.caption: ODD NUMBERS

scenes.text: Here's how to do it in five minutes. Take everything off your mantel. Everything. Wipe it clean. Then put back only your tallest piece first, on the left third of the mantel, not dead center. Then put a medium piece on the right. Then fill in with small things, low and close to the garland. Step back to the door and look. Move one thing. Look again. That's all decorators do.
scenes.query: woman stepping back looking at mantel
scenes.caption: STEP BACK AND LOOK

scenes.text: Mistake number two. A skinny garland. One thin strand of fake pine lying flat on a mantel looks sad and cheap. The fix is to layer. Lay down your cheap garland first, then tuck real cuttings into it. Pine, cedar, a little holly, even branches from the bottom of your Christmas tree. It makes it full and fat, and the real ones make the whole room smell like Christmas.
scenes.caption: LAYER IT

scenes.text: And let it hang over the ends, sweetheart. Don't stop the garland right at the edges of the mantel. Let it drape down a foot or so on each side, like a waterfall. That's the difference between a garland that looks like an afterthought and one that looks like it belongs there. Tie it down with fishing line, so nothing shows.
scenes.caption: LET IT DRAPE

scenes.text: Mistake number three. Too many little things. Every ornament, every snow globe, every figurine you own, all crowded together. It looks cluttered, and nothing stands out. Pick one idea, honey. All brass and greenery. All white and silver. All red and wood. Put the rest away for next year, and the mantel will look calm and rich.
scenes.caption: PICK ONE IDEA

scenes.text: If this is helping you, tap the like button for me, sweetheart. It helps Grandma more than you know. And here's my rule. If you can count more than eleven separate things on your mantel, take three off. Go ahead. Count yours tonight. I'll bet you have twenty. I'll tell you in a minute where those extra things should go instead.
scenes.caption: COUNT TO ELEVEN

scenes.text: Here's a little trick for anything you love that didn't make the cut. Make a Christmas tray. A big wooden cutting board or a silver tray, with your snow globes, a little candle, and a few sprigs of pine, all grouped together on the coffee table. Grouped together, little things look like a collection. Scattered, they look like clutter. Same things, honey. Different home.
scenes.query: tray of Christmas decorations coffee table
scenes.caption: A CHRISTMAS TRAY

scenes.text: Mistake number four. Forgetting the wall above the mantel. Your mantel is only half the picture. Hang a wreath above it, or lean a big mirror or a framed picture behind it. A mirror is the best, because it doubles the candlelight and the tree lights. My mother hung her wreath on a ribbon from the top of the wall, so it floated over the mantel like a picture.
scenes.caption: LOOK UP

scenes.text: So far, a triangle not a line, a fat garland, one idea, and something on the wall. Mistake number five. Mismatched, saggy stockings hanging every which way. Hang them evenly spaced, at the same height. And if your stockings don't match, tie the same red ribbon or the same little tag on every one. Suddenly they look like a set.
scenes.caption: EVENLY SPACED

scenes.text: And please, honey, be careful. If your fireplace works, never hang stockings or garland over a burning fire, and never use real candles near a dry garland. A Christmas fire is the most common way a house burns in December. My neighbor lost her whole living room in nineteen seventy-eight to one candle and one dry pine branch.
scenes.query: fireplace safety stockings away from fire
scenes.caption: BE CAREFUL

scenes.text: And here's the stocking holder trick. If you don't have proper stocking hangers, take a long wooden board, paint it, and screw cup hooks into the bottom. Lay it on the mantel and set a few heavy things on top, like your candlesticks and books. It holds every stocking, nothing falls, and it doesn't scratch your mantel. My son-in-law made ours in twenty minutes in nineteen ninety.
scenes.caption: THE BOARD TRICK

scenes.text: Mistake number six. A mantel with nothing alive on it. All plastic and glitter. Add one living thing, sweetheart. A bowl of red apples or oranges. A potted amaryllis. Fresh cranberries in a glass jar with water and a floating candle. It makes the mantel look like a real home, where real people live. And remember those extra things you took off? Put them on a side table, grouped together. They'll look better there anyway.
scenes.query: red apples bowl cranberries jar mantel
scenes.caption: ONE LIVING THING

scenes.text: And now mistake number seven, the trick I promised you. Only decorating for the daytime. Most people see your mantel at night, by lamplight. So my mother put little votive candles in plain glass jars, all along the mantel, tucked down in the greenery. At night, she turned off the overhead light and lit them, and the whole mantel glowed like a church at midnight.
scenes.query: votive candles glowing in greenery night
scenes.caption: IT GLOWED

scenes.text: Today, honey, use the little battery candles with timers. They look real, they're safe near the garland, and they come on by themselves at five o'clock every evening. Get a dozen of them for about ten dollars. Tuck them in, set the timer, and every night your living room will look like a Christmas card. It's the cheapest trick there is, and nobody ever does it.
scenes.query: battery candles in mantel garland at night
scenes.caption: TEN DOLLARS

scenes.text: And one last thing. Don't forget the hearth, sweetheart, the floor in front of the fireplace. That's where a big basket of pinecones, a stack of firewood tied with a red ribbon, or a big lantern goes. It grounds the whole picture. A beautiful mantel floating above an empty floor looks unfinished. Fill that bottom corner, and suddenly the whole wall looks complete.
scenes.query: basket of pinecones by hearth firewood
scenes.caption: DON'T FORGET THE HEARTH

scenes.text: My mother put an old milk can on our hearth, painted red, filled with tall pine branches and a few branches of red berries from the hedge. When the minister came for his Christmas visit, he sat on our couch and stared at that milk can, and he asked her where she'd bought it. She said, Reverend, I bought it from the cow. He laughed for ten minutes.
scenes.query: red painted milk can with pine branches
scenes.caption: FROM THE COW

scenes.text: So one more time. Build a triangle, not a line, in odd numbers. Layer real greenery into your garland and let it drape. Pick one idea. Hang something on the wall above. Space the stockings evenly. Add one living thing. And put little candles in the greenery for the night. That's a mantel your family will remember.
scenes.caption: A MANTEL TO REMEMBER

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. What's the one thing that always goes on your mantel at Christmas? I'd love to hear it. The whole playlist of Grandma's Christmas tips is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey.
scenes.caption: WHAT'S ON YOURS?
